questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of productivity?
options: Output per unit of input per period of time
The total output of a business
Producing at the minimum average cost
The maximum output a business can produce
questions.why: Productivity is a ratio of output to input, most often output per worker. Production is total output; efficiency is minimum average cost; capacity is the maximum possible.
whyNot: That is production.
That is efficiency.
That is capacity.

questions.stem: A workshop produces 7,200 units a month with 24 employees. What is labour productivity?
questions.why: Labour productivity = total output / number of employees = 7,200 / 24 = 300 units per employee per month.
whyNot: This multiplies instead of dividing.
This divides employees by output, the wrong way round.
That is the number of employees.

questions.stem: Which production method involves producing one item at a time to a customer's specific requirements?
questions.why: Job production is bespoke: tailoring, construction, one-off engineering. Highest unit cost, highest flexibility.
whyNot: Batch production makes groups of identical items, then switches.
Flow production makes large volumes of a standardised product continuously.
Cell production divides the process into teams owning a complete stage.

questions.stem: Which production method gives the lowest unit cost but the least flexibility?
questions.why: A continuous standardised line achieves the lowest cost per unit through scale and specialisation, and it cannot easily change what it makes.
whyNot: Job production is the most flexible and most expensive per unit.
Batch sits between the two on both measures.
Cell production is moderately flexible with moderate unit costs.

questions.stem: Why does cell production tend to improve motivation?
options: Teams own a complete stage, so the work is varied and the output is identifiable
Workers are paid more in cell production
Cells have no supervision at all
questions.why: Rather than repeating one task on a line, the team is responsible for a whole section. That is job enrichment in Herzberg's terms, and it also improves quality because the team can see and fix its own problems.
whyNot: Pay is a separate decision.
Cells are still managed; they have more autonomy, not none.
Headcount depends on the work, not the layout.

questions.stem: Labour costs are $48,000 a month. Output rises from 7,200 to 9,000 units with the same staff. What happens to labour cost per unit?
questions.why: 48,000 / 7,200 = $6.67. 48,000 / 9,000 = $5.33. Higher productivity with the same wage bill cuts unit labour cost by about 20%, which feeds straight into either a lower price or a wider margin.
whyNot: This reverses the two figures.
The same cost spread over more units must give a lower cost per unit.

questions.stem: How can a business raise productivity and become less efficient at the same time?
options: If the equipment that raised output cost more than the labour it saved
If output falls at the same time
questions.why: Productivity is output per input; efficiency is minimum average cost. New machinery can raise output per worker while raising total cost per unit, so the two measures move in opposite directions. Making this distinction is a strong exam point.
whyNot: They measure different things, so they can diverge.
Falling output would reduce productivity too.
More workers with the same output would lower productivity.

questions.stem: Which type of production is a guesthouse closest to?
options: Job production, because each guest's stay is handled individually
Flow production, because rooms are standardised
Batch production, because guests arrive in groups
Cell production, because staff work in teams
questions.why: Each stay is individually delivered rather than produced as standardised output, which is why unit costs are high and service quality, and therefore staff, matter so much.
whyNot: Rooms may be similar, and the service delivered is not standardised or continuous.
Arrival patterns are not a production method.
Teams may be used, and the output is still individual rather than a repeated process stage.

questions.stem: When is capital-intensive production most appropriate?
options: High volume, standardised output and high wage costs
Low volume, bespoke output and low wage costs
When the business has very little finance
questions.why: Machinery needs volume to justify the investment, and it is most attractive where labour is expensive. It is inflexible, so variable demand argues against it.
whyNot: Those conditions favour labour-intensive production.
Capital intensity is inflexible, so variable demand is a problem.
It requires heavy upfront investment.

questions.stem: Why is a short product lead-in time a competitive advantage?
options: The business reaches the market first, can charge a premium before rivals arrive, and responds faster to changing tastes
It reduces the cost of raw materials
It removes the need for market research
questions.why: Speed to market is an advantage in its own right, not just an operational detail. First movers set the standard and earn at a premium before competition catches up.
whyNot: Material costs are unrelated to development speed.
Research is still needed, and arguably faster.
Speed and quality are separate, and rushing can reduce quality.
